newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan official tries to reassure edgy markets.
newsitem.headline: Japan official tries to reassure edgy markets.

text.p: A top Japanese finance official, seeking to halt the pounding given to Tokyo shares and the yen, said on Sunday that financial markets were too pessimistic about Japan's economy.
Eisuke Sakakibara, dubbed "Mr. Yen" for his impact on markets, also denied there was disagreement between Japan and the other major economies over exchange rate policy, which has unnerved investors.
"The economy is not in as bad a shape as the market thinks," Sakakibara, influential director general of the ministry's international finance bureau, said in a television interview.
"I think Japanese people should stop selling out their own markets."
Sakakibara made his reassuring remarks as Japanese stocks and currency braced for another volatile week.
On Friday, the Nikkei average of 225 leading shares fell 1.23 percent to close at 17,689.36. The dollar hit a fresh 47-month high, rising above 120 yen in late Tokyo trading.
Sakakibara threw his weight behind a proposal to remove the securities transaction tax, which is currently imposed on all deals in stocks, bonds and money markets.

"To be on an equal footing with banks overseas, the tax bureau should decide the fate of the current withholding and securities transaction tax in time for the next fiscal year tax review period," he said.
Last week, Tokyo stocks rebounded slightly on market excitement over prospects that the government would scrap the securities transaction tax by 1998.
Sakakibara also dimissed as groundless recent market speculation that Japan may be in a conflict with the United States and other industrialised nations over where exchange rates should be.
"The talk that there is a difference of opinion among monetary authorities of Japan, United States and Germany over foreign exchange rates is an uninformed theory," he said.
Japan's market slide has also sparked concern among ruling and opposition party lawmakers, who said on Sunday that Japan's banks need to disclose the extent of their bad loans.
The lawmakers also said public funds should be considered as a way to solve the bad loan problem.
The once-mighty Japanese banking industry has been groaning under a mountain of bad loans. One opposition lawmaker said some analysts estimate the burden could reach 100 trillion yen.
The finance ministry's official estimate of problem loans among deposit-taking financial institutions is 23 trillion yen.

In a separate televised news programme, ruling Liberal Democratic Party secretary Koichi Kato and top members of the opposition Democratic and Shinshinto parties agreed the use of public funds should be discussed, but did not specify how.
"This is an interesting point which they raised, which could spark new debate in how Japan tackles the banks' bad loan problem," a trader for a major brokerage said.
The government has in the past used public funds to close out failed mortgage firms, but the move drew public outcry.
Sakakibara also said that a schedule for Japan's long-awaited "Big Bang" deregulation of markets and the economy would be released this summer.
But he warned banks would be hit hard by the measures.
"(The Big Bang) will be a major surgery and (Japanese banks) should be ready for much bloodletting," he said.

It was the first time an official has said when a schedule for the deregulation package would be announced. Japan has said the plan, intended to revitalise the sluggish economy and its financial markets, will be carried out by 2001.
